passage: In the hostel common room, the new Class 11 batch sat in a circle for the welcome evening. Leela, who had arrived from Shillong that morning, kept tucking the same strand of hair behind her ear, smoothing her kurta, then lifting her phone and staring at the dark screen as if it held something important. When her turn came to introduce herself, Ujjwal called out, "Mirror, mirror on the wall!" A few people laughed. Leela's ears turned red and she mumbled her name so quietly that the warden asked her to repeat it. Ujjwal saw her shoulders fold in and the phone go back up in front of her face. At dinner he slid his tray next to hers. "That was a rubbish joke. First day's hard enough. Shillong, right? Tell me about it?" Leela lowered the phone.

qa.q: Where had Leela arrived from?
qa.a: Shillong.

qa.q: What might Leela's hair-tucking and phone-staring suggest?
qa.a: Leela probably felt self-conscious and nervous on her first evening among strangers, though some of it may have been ordinary grooming.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal repair things?
qa.a: He called his own joke rubbish, said first days are hard, and asked Leela about Shillong, giving her a friendly way in.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt seeing Leela's shoulders fold in?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely felt sorry and uncomfortable, seeing that his joke had deepened her embarrassment.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager fixing hair and hiding behind a phone when watched, and teasing about it deepening her insecurity.

subtype: Touching the face and neck under stress [Regulating]
passage: In the clubhouse of Green Park Apartments in Hyderabad, Ankita waited to present the youth committee's composting plan to thirty residents. She rubbed the back of her neck, touched her cheek, and nibbled the edge of a thumbnail. Ayesha, beside her with the slides, whispered, "Stop that. Mr Reddy will think you're hiding something about the survey numbers." Ankita pulled her hand down. "I'm not hiding anything. My hands just want something to do." "Then give them something better. Remember what Ms Fernandes told us before the debate?" They both breathed in slowly through the nose and out even more slowly, twice. Ankita's shoulders loosened. When her name was called, she walked up, rested her hands on the podium and began: "Forty-two families said yes."

qa.q: How many residents were at the meeting?
qa.a: Thirty.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling while rubbing her neck and nibbling her thumbnail?
qa.a: Ankita felt nervous before presenting; the self-touches were a way of calming the nerves, not hiding anything.

qa.q: What helped Ankita more than just stopping the touches?
qa.a: Two slow breaths, which loosened her shoulders, and resting her hands on the podium.

qa.q: How did Ayesha think the residents might read Ankita's self-touching?
qa.a: Ayesha worried Mr Reddy would take it as a sign that Ankita was hiding something about the survey, though it was only nerves.

grounding: It shows a teenager touching the face and neck to calm nerves before a presentation, the touches being no sign of hidden thoughts, and slow breathing helping more.

passage: I'm Pankaj, and I sit next to Aparna at tuition. On Tuesday she got a low mark on her physics test, and I squeezed her shoulder for a second. She gave me a small smile; that seemed fine to both of us. Later, the tuition owner's assistant, a grown man, came round checking answers and kept his hand on her upper back for a long time while he talked, then moved it lower. Aparna went completely stiff. Then she said loudly, "Please don't touch me," and pulled her chair away. He laughed and moved on. After class she walked straight to her mother at the gate and told her. I stayed with them. Her mother listened, said, "You did exactly right, and it's not your fault," and phoned the owner there and then. The owner said the assistant would be kept away from students at once, and that evening her mother reported it to the police helpline too.

qa.q: What did Aparna say to the assistant?
qa.a: "Please don't touch me."

qa.q: What might Aparna's going completely stiff suggest?
qa.a: Aparna was probably uncomfortable and frightened by the long touch that moved lower, very different from Pankaj's brief squeeze.

qa.q: Which steps were right, and how did the adults respond?
qa.a: Saying stop, moving away and telling her mother; her mother believed her, phoned the owner, who kept the assistant away from students, and reported it that evening.

qa.q: What would change if Aparna had stayed silent to avoid a scene?
qa.a: The assistant might have gone on touching her or others, and no adult would have known to act.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager telling a friend's brief supportive squeeze apart from an unwelcome touch by an adult in power, saying stop and telling a trusted adult who acts that day, as seen by a classmate.

passage:
Monday: At the farewell for their music teacher, Jagdish threw his arms round everyone, including Sarita. She went rigid. "Sorry, I'm not a hugger." Jagdish stepped back and muttered, "Wow. Okay. Sorry for caring," and walked off.
Wednesday: At dinner he told his mother about it, expecting her to take his side. She put her spoon down. "Sarita told you what she likes. Then you made her feel bad for saying it. That's pressure, even if you didn't mean it." Jagdish's face went hot. "So I'm a creep?" "No. You're someone who can ask first."
Saturday: After the concert, Jagdish went up to Sarita. "Hug, high five, or nothing?" Sarita grinned and held up her palm. "High five." It landed with a loud smack. "And sorry about Monday," he said. "Thanks," she said.

qa.q: What did Jagdish offer Sarita after the concert?
qa.a: Hug, high five, or nothing.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he muttered "Sorry for caring"?
qa.a: He felt rejected and embarrassed, and turned that hurt into a guilt-trip.

qa.q: What changed in how Jagdish approached closeness?
qa.a: He talked it through with his mother, then asked first and offered choices, accepted Sarita's pick, and apologised 🙂

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt when Jagdish walked off?
qa.a: Sarita probably felt uncomfortable and guilty for stating a simple preference, which is exactly what the pressure did.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning to ask before hugging and to accept 'I'm not a hugger' without guilt-tripping, after talking it over with a trusted adult.

subtype: Approaching and stepping back in social ties [Mismatch]
passage:
Class teacher's note, 11C, week 6
Over the past fortnight, Leela has moved from the back row next to Kiran to the front bench beside Tanvi's group. In the staffroom a colleague remarked that Leela had "upgraded to the popular crowd". Kiran has looked hurt; he now eats lunch alone and hangs back when Leela passes. I did not want to guess, so today I asked each of them separately. Leela said her new glasses still aren't right and she cannot read the board from the back; she misses sitting with Kiran but thought he had gone cold on her. Kiran said he stepped back because he assumed she didn't want him around. Neither had said a word to the other. Next step: I have moved Kiran to the second bench, next to Leela's, and suggested they sort out lunch themselves.

qa.q: Why did Leela move to the front bench?
qa.a: Her new glasses still aren't right and she can't read the board from the back.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling as he hung back when Leela passed?
qa.a: Kiran felt hurt and left out, assuming Leela didn't want him around.

qa.q: Why was the teacher right to ask instead of guessing?
qa.a: Asking each of them separately showed that eyesight, not rivalry, explained the move, and that both had misread the other's distance.

qa.q: How did the colleague read Leela's move?
qa.a: The colleague saw it as Leela moving up to the popular crowd, a quick conclusion that turned out to be wrong.

grounding: It illustrates teenagers moving closer to some peers and away from others, and distance being misread as popularity or coldness until someone asks.

passage:
Akash: that guy from the gym did it again
Ojas: the one who stands right behind you at the water cooler?
Akash: yeah. I stepped back and put my bag between us and he just stepped closer
Akash: then he followed me to the bus stop. didn't say anything. just stood there
Ojas: that's not ok. you made it super clear
Akash: maybe I'm overthinking
Ojas: you're not. you stepped away and he kept coming. that's the line
Ojas: tell your dad tonight. not tomorrow
Akash: he's home. showing him this chat now
Akash: Ojas, this is Akash's father. Thank you for telling him to talk to me. I've called the gym manager, who is checking the cameras tonight, and I'll pick Akash up from now on.
Ojas: thank you uncle

qa.q: Where did the man follow Akash to?
qa.a: The bus stop.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he wrote "maybe I'm overthinking"?
qa.a: Akash felt uneasy and unsure, doubting the discomfort even though the man kept closing in.

qa.q: What did Akash's father do after reading the chat?
qa.a: He thanked Ojas, called the gym manager, who is checking the cameras that night, and arranged to pick Akash up from now on.

qa.q: How did Ojas see the situation?
qa.a: Ojas saw that Akash had given clear signals and the man ignored them, so it had crossed a line and needed an adult that night.

grounding: It shows a teenager stepping back and putting a bag in between when someone stands too close and follows him, and a trusted adult being told the same night.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
"Tarun, is that phone from a museum?" Vikram held it up. "Does it take calls from the dinosaurs?"
The group roared. Kishore laughed too, a beat late and a little too loud.
Tarun laughed loudest of all. "Ha, yeah, my Jurassic phone."
"Does it run on coal?" someone added.
"Probably!" Tarun's laugh went higher. He took the phone back and put it face down.
Kishore's stomach tightened. Last week Tarun had told him his dad had lost his job.
"Okay," Kishore said, not loudly. "That's not funny anymore. Come on, the match starts in five."
Vikram rolled his eyes. "Relax, it's a joke."
"It was a joke three jokes ago."
On the way to the ground, Tarun fell into step beside him. "Thanks," he muttered. "I didn't know how to stop laughing."

qa.q: What did Vikram ask whether the phone could take calls from?
qa.a: The dinosaurs.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he laughed a beat late?
qa.a: Kishore felt uneasy and tense, laughing to fit in while knowing the joke touched something painful for Tarun.

qa.q: What made Kishore's boundary work?
qa.a: He said calmly, not loudly, that it wasn't funny anymore and gave everyone somewhere to go, without shaming anyone.

qa.q: What was the joking like for Tarun?
qa.a: It hurt, but Tarun laughed loudest to protect his place in the group and didn't know how to stop.

grounding: It illustrates teenagers laughing along with an unkind group joke to fit in or hide hurt, and one of them setting a calm 'that's not funny' boundary.

passage:
Tuesday
Worst thing ever: I LAUGHED when Mrs Kapoor told our group we'd be marked down for copying the lab report. Not a fun laugh. It just burst out like a hiccup and I couldn't stop it. She went red and said, "You find this funny, Sharmila?" and sent me to stand outside. I wanted to disappear.
At break Anjali found me by the water cooler. She said, "You laughed like that when your Dadi's cat died. I don't think it's funny for you. Are you scared?" And I burst into tears, because yes, I was terrified of what Papa would say.
Anjali said I should explain to Mrs Kapoor. After school I did, with Anjali standing beside me. Mrs Kapoor listened and said she had misread it. She still marked us down, but she said sorry for sending me out.
Sharmila

qa.q: Why was the group being marked down?
qa.a: For copying the lab report.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling behind the laugh?
qa.a: Sharmila was scared and embarrassed, terrified of what Papa would say; the laugh was stress bursting out, not amusement.

qa.q: What helped clear up the misreading?
qa.a: Anjali's gentle question about fear, then Sharmila explaining to Mrs Kapoor after school with Anjali there, which led Mrs Kapoor to apologise.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kapoor read the laugh at first?
qa.a: Mrs Kapoor took it as mockery and disrespect, so she sent Sharmila outside.

grounding: It shows a teenager's nervous laughter while being scolded being read as disrespect, and a gentle check on feelings revealing fear.

passage: Chaitanya, stop apologising. I know you asked if I was sad at the farewell. Listen, this is Minakshi explaining herself, which is rare, so pay attention. When Ravi did his impression of Principal Ma'am, I laughed so hard I was crying. Real tears, runny nose, everything. Happy tears. Then later, when I told you how Coach dropped me from the relay without saying why, I was crying again, but I wasn't sad then either. I was furious. My voice shakes and my eyes leak when I'm angry, and people think I'm weak. So when you said, "Aww, don't be sad," it made me angrier, not better. I'm not mad at you. Next time, just ask, "What kind of tears are these?" I'll tell you. Probably while crying.

qa.q: What did Ravi do at the farewell?
qa.a: An impression of Principal Ma'am.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling while crying about the relay?
qa.a: Minakshi was furious at being dropped without a reason; the tears came with anger, not sadness.

qa.q: What does Minakshi ask Chaitanya to do next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To ask 'What kind of tears are these?', because tears can mean joy, anger or overwhelm, and labelling them from outside can be wrong 🙂

qa.q: How did Chaitanya read Minakshi's tears?
qa.a: Chaitanya took them as sadness and said 'Aww, don't be sad', which missed the anger and made it worse.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager crying from laughter and from anger, and why asking about mixed tears beats labelling them from outside.

passage:
Warden's note, hostel Block B, Thursday night
At 10.30 pm, Bhavna came to my room. Her roommate, Aditi, has been crying silently under her blanket most nights this week and has stopped going to dinner and to the dance club she loved. I went up with Bhavna straight away. Aditi was curled under the blanket, very still. I sat on the edge of the bed and waited. After a while she said, "Nothing's going to get better here." I did not argue or lecture. I said I was glad Bhavna had come for me, that Aditi was not in any trouble, and that I would stay. With her agreement I phoned her mother that night, and they talked for twenty minutes. I checked on her again at midnight; she was asleep. Next steps: the counsellor will see her at 8 am, and I have told Bhavna to come to me any time.

qa.q: What time did Bhavna come to the warden's room?
qa.a: At 10.30 pm.

qa.q: What might Aditi's words "Nothing's going to get better here" suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Aditi seemed hopeless and lonely, worn down after a week of hidden crying and pulling back from dinner and dance.

qa.q: Which of the warden's steps mattered most that night?
qa.a: Going up at once, staying calmly without lecturing, phoning Aditi's mother that night, checking again at midnight, and booking the counsellor for the morning.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt going to the warden?
qa.a: Bhavna was probably worried about Aditi and unsure whether speaking up was right; the warden's quick response showed it was.

grounding: It shows a teenager's frequent silent crying with withdrawal and hopeless words being taken to a trusted adult who responds the same night and involves a counsellor.
